Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
3) Global memory notes are advisory and must not override current instructions.

agree.point: OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic each say a compaction item does not carry everything, so some things must be sent again after it: tools added mid-conversation (OpenAI), the system prompt (xAI), mid-conversation instructions and attachments (Anthropic).

basis.quote: The explicit trigger's compaction item doesn't carry earlier `additional_tools` declarations. If you resume from that item, supply the tools you need in the request's `tools` array or append a new developer `additional_tools` item before the user message.

A compaction item has to come first, because the API drops anything before it, `instructions` included. So the system prompt stays out of the compaction and goes right after the item, which keeps the handbook word for word however often the chat is compacted.
If an instruction or effort level still matters, state it again in a `role: "system"` message.
Images, documents, `container_upload` blocks, and fetched URLs inside the summarized messages are gone once the block replaces them. Restate or re-upload anything a later turn still needs.

differ.point: Google says its large window invites the more direct approach of providing all relevant information up front. OpenAI says putting everything into a long context costs accuracy and must be evaluated at different context sizes, and Anthropic says more context is not automatically better because accuracy and recall degrade as tokens grow.

basis.quote: While these techniques remain valuable in specific scenarios, Gemini's extensive context window invites a more direct approach: providing all relevant information upfront.
This illustrates the problem with long-context - it promises a much simpler retrieval process where you can dump everything in context, but at a cost in accuracy.

A larger context window allows the model to handle more complex and lengthy prompts, but more context isn’t automatically better. As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as *context rot*. This makes curating what’s in context just as important as how much space is available.

Long-context models allow prompt engineering to scale further - however, beware that models can struggle to maintain attention across very large prompts with complex instructions, and so you should always pair long context models with evaluation at different context sizes to ensure you don’t get [**lost in the middle**](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172).

differ.point: OpenAI's compaction item is opaque and not meant to be read by people. Anthropic's compaction block holds the summary as readable text with a signature, and Anthropic lets the caller replace the summarisation prompt.

basis.quote: The returned compaction item carries forward key prior state and reasoning into the next run using fewer tokens. It is opaque and not intended to be human-interpretable.
The block holds the summary as text you can read, and a signature. Send it in future requests exactly as it came.

[Write your own summarization prompt](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction-on-demand#write-your-own-summarization-prompt): when the default summary drops something a later turn needs. Your prompt replaces the default one.

differ.point: xAI advises a smaller, faster model for the compaction call when compacting often. Anthropic's server-side compaction always summarises with the request's own model and offers no cheaper one.

basis.quote: Pick a smaller / faster model for compaction if you are doing it frequently.
**Same model for summarization:** The model specified in your request is used for summarization. There is no option to use a different (for example, cheaper) model for the summary.

differ.point: Compaction triggers differ: Google's managed agent compacts at about 135k tokens, Grok Build at 85% of the window, Claude Code at about 967K tokens on 1M-window models, and Anthropic's API threshold cannot be set below 50,000 tokens. On timing, OpenAI says to compact after major milestones and not every turn, xAI suggests every N turns or a chosen threshold, and Anthropic says to try later compaction points.

basis.quote: - **Context compaction:** Automatic context compaction (triggered at ~135k tokens) to support long-running, multi-turn sessions without losing context or hitting token limits.
| `auto_compact_threshold_percent` | `[session]` | `0–100` (default `85`) | Auto-compact when context usage reaches this percent. |
Models running with a native 1M window compact before the window fills, at about 967K tokens by default.
Compact after major milestones rather than every turn. Keep the prompt functionally consistent after compaction and treat compacted items as opaque state.
When to trigger compaction. `input_tokens` is the only supported trigger type. `value` must be at least 50,000 tokens.
A typical pattern is to call the Compaction API every N turns inside an agent loop, or once whenever your bookkeeping shows the rendered context above a threshold you've chosen for your workload.
Compacting early to save cost can be the wrong trade-off between cost and intelligence, so experiment with later compaction points.

differ.point: Placement around a summary differs: OpenAI says a home-grown compacted item goes at the end of the context and not before recent turns, Anthropic says to put the block in front of the turns that were kept, and xAI says the item must come first because the API drops everything before it, instructions included.

basis.quote: **Custom compaction:** If you use a different or home-grown compaction strategy, place the compacted item at the end of the model’s context, instead of before recent turns.
The API summarizes every message it is sent, so send only the older turns, then put the block in front of the turns you kept.

A compaction item has to come first, because the API drops anything before it, `instructions` included. So the system prompt stays out of the compaction and goes right after the item, which keeps the handbook word for word however often the chat is compacted.

differ.point: What server-side state carries differs: on OpenAI a developer message in the first input stays in the chained history, while Google's Interactions API says request parameters must be re-specified in every new interaction.

basis.quote: A `developer` message in the initial `input` stays in the chained history. Top-level `instructions` apply only to the request that supplies them, so you can give a follow-up response its own guidance.
This means you must re-specify these parameters in each new interaction if you want them to apply.

differ.point: For a long session, OpenAI's Codex guidance is to stay in the same chat and compact while the objective is unchanged, forking only when it diverges. Anthropic says to consider a brand new context window that rediscovers state from files instead of compacting, which depends on the handoff artifact holding enough state.

basis.quote: Keep one chat per coherent unit of work. If the work is still part of the same problem, staying in the same chat is often better because it preserves the reasoning trail. Fork only when the work truly branches.

When a context window is cleared, consider starting with a brand new context window rather than using compaction. Claude’s latest models are extremely effective at discovering state from the local filesystem.
The practical sequence is: Check status, compact when the objective is still the same, and fork when the objective has diverged.

While compaction preserves continuity, it doesn't give the agent a clean slate, which means context anxiety can still persist. A reset provides a clean slate, at the cost of the handoff artifact having enough state for the next agent to pick up the work cleanly.

practices.statement: Give each role only the context kinds its role row declares, and have the controller refuse a prompt that carries an undeclared or withheld kind. Keep state that only the controller needs out of every prompt.
practices.why: OpenAI says to keep runtime-only state out of the model's context, and Google and Anthropic both say to leave out tokens the model does not need for the task.
practices.today: contextFor() passes a role only its declared context kinds, throws on an undeclared kind and on a withheld kind nested inside a permitted value, with a test. Its stated limit is free text that merely mentions a plan.

basis.quote: If the model needs a fact, put it in instructions, input, retrieval, or a tool. If only your runtime needs it, keep it in local context.
Generally, if you don't need tokens to be passed to the model, it is best to avoid passing them.
If Claude doesn’t need it to perform the task, don’t include it.

Do not dump all the fields from internal systems into the profile section. Make sure that every single token you add here helps the agent make better decisions. Some of these fields might instead be input parameters to a tool call that you can pass from the state object without making them visible to the model.
find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome.

practices.statement: Give every seat a bounded, curated dossier up front plus read-only retrieval for the rest, and extend that retrieval to the implementer. List in the dossier what was left out so a seat knows what it can ask for.
practices.why: Anthropic describes loading some data up front and letting the agent load the rest by reference with tools, and OpenAI says to give the agent files to inspect instead of pasting large documents into the prompt.
practices.today: The planner, plan reviewers, change reviewers and validator get an evidence dossier that lists what is left out, and may answer with read-only retrieval requests. The implementer gets the carried plan in its goal but has no retrieval.

basis.quote: In certain settings, the most effective agents might employ a hybrid strategy, retrieving some data up front for speed, and pursuing further autonomous exploration at its discretion.
Instead of pasting large documents into context, mount them into the sandbox and let the agent work with files.

Rather than pre-processing all relevant data up front, agents built with the “just in time” approach maintain lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, web links, etc.) and use these references to dynamically load data into context at runtime using tools.
Agent workflows get brittle when the model needs that kind of workspace but only receives prompt context.
Share the information that could change the result. Add only the sources that matter, and explain what ChatGPT should take from each one.

practices.statement: Bound every evidence view, tool result, test output and diff in bytes or tokens before it enters a prompt. When something is cut, give the seat a continuation request or file path for the remainder instead of dropping it silently.
practices.why: OpenAI says to shorten long tool outputs before they are first sent, xAI caps result rows because they go into context, and Codex and Claude Code both replace oversized output with a saved file the model can read.
practices.today: Tests show byte bounds on the dossier, on each retrieval result and on a seat's whole investigation, with a 'next' request that continues a cut result; verify output and diffs shown to the reviewer are also bounded. The framing around each result is not counted against the budget.

basis.quote: We strongly recommend either using compaction, or shortening long tool outputs and downsizing images or files before they’re sent to the model for the first time.
It returns at most 100 rows, and fewer if they're long, since they go into Grok's context.

when a successful result with no image content exceeds the token limit, Claude Code saves it to a file and replaces it in the conversation with a message that names the file path, so Claude reads the file when it needs the content.

By default, Codex limits each model-visible hook-output message to roughly 2,500 tokens. If a hook returns more, Codex saves the full text under `<temp_dir>/hook_outputs/<session_id>/<uuid>.txt` and gives the model a head-and-tail preview with the saved-file path.
The test harness should not print thousands of useless bytes. At most, it should print a few lines of output and log all important information to a file so Claude can find it when needed.

practices.statement: Admit a provider call only when input plus reserved output and reasoning tokens fit the model's recorded window, counting cached prefixes as input, and refuse a model with no recorded window. Record per model any lower ceiling a provider or gateway enforces.
practices.why: OpenAI and Google say input, output and reasoning share one window, Anthropic and Google say cached tokens still count toward it, and Claude Code cannot detect a lower gateway limit unless it is set explicitly.
practices.today: The model client admits a request only when input tokens plus reserved output fit the recorded window, refuses an unknown window and holds an input ceiling for one model, with a test. The survey does not say the reserve covers reasoning tokens, and seat selection estimates context as characters divided by 4.

basis.quote: This max tokens number includes input, output, and reasoning tokens.
In Gemini 4 (`gemini-4-carbon`, `gemini-4-argon`, `gemini-4-neon`, and `gemini-4-hydrogen`), the 1M-token context window is **shared across input, thinking, and output tokens**

Cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window: [prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count.
The model doesn't make any distinction between cached tokens and regular input tokens. Cached content is a prefix to the prompt.

Claude Code can't detect a lower limit that the gateway or the server behind it enforces. If your gateway rejects requests above 200K tokens, set [`CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=200000`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) in the environment that starts Claude Code

practices.statement: Keep every seat conversation append-only: replay each model output item exactly as received, reasoning and thinking included, and never edit the system prompt, tools or earlier messages mid-conversation. On OpenAI, change instructions by appending a new developer message.
practices.why: All four labs say to pass prior output back unchanged, and OpenAI and Anthropic say edits to the prefix drop or invalidate the model's earlier reasoning.
practices.today: Anthropic and Google seats are replay only, with the conversation text in a separate history file and a hash chain on the seat record. The survey shows code but no test that replayed items are unmodified, and says the record does not prove the vendor's server-side conversation matches it.

basis.quote: To get the best performance from our models, we recommend avoiding changes to the prefix and adopting an append-only integration pattern as far as possible.
It edits, reorders, or filters output items before sending them back. Pass them back exactly as received.

If the model uses "thinking" or tools, you **must** preserve and resend all model-generated steps (such as `thought` and `function_call` steps) exactly as received, as they contain signatures required to continue the conversation.

Keep the conversation append-only (no edits to the `system` prompt, `tools`, or earlier messages mid-conversation) so the thinking blocks pass the [prefix check](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/preserved-thinking/prefix-checks#prefix-check).
When you want to update those instructions, append a _new_ `developer` message at the end of the model's context instead of changing the initial developer message.

practices.statement: Use one continuation strategy per seat conversation and never mix replay with server-held state. For OpenAI and xAI seats that continue by response id, also keep the original input and full output locally so the conversation can be rebuilt after the 30-day retention or when an id cannot be resolved.
practices.why: OpenAI says mixing local replay with server-managed state duplicates context, and OpenAI and xAI both store responses for 30 days and say to resend full context when a stored id is gone.
practices.today: OpenAI and xAI seats default to server-side previous_response_id with replay as a toggle, so one strategy applies per vendor. The seat record never holds text, and the survey describes a local history file only for the replay-only Anthropic and Google seats.

basis.quote: In most applications, pick one strategy per conversation. Mixing local replay with server-managed state can duplicate context unless you are deliberately reconciling both layers.
**The responses will be stored for 30 days, after which they will be removed. This means you can use the response ID to retrieve or continue a conversation within 30 days of sending the request.**
Response objects are saved for 30 days by default.
If an uncached ID cannot be resolved, send a new turn with `previous_response_id` set to `null` and pass full input context.
If your app may need to continue after the response expires, save the original input and the full response `output` while you can still retrieve it.

practices.statement: Give every replayed or chained seat a compaction path, not one model only, triggered at a controller-set limit below that model's window and never with a tool call open. Set the limit per lab, since OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic each expose a compaction call that needs the conversation to still fit, while the Google records describe compaction only inside the managed agent.
practices.why: OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic say compaction cannot rescue a conversation already over the limit, Anthropic says to choose a limit below the window and rejects an open tool call, and Google's managed agent compacts on its own at about 135k tokens.
practices.today: Compaction exists for one model: a claude-fable-5-2 replay history that reaches 512,000 bytes of JSON is replaced by one signed compaction block, and an unresolved tool turn is not compacted, with a test. No other model or lab has a compaction path.

basis.quote: The window you send to `/responses/compact` must still fit within your model's context window.
The current window still fits within the model's context limit (compaction shrinks the conversation — it cannot rescue a request that is already over the limit).
Compare that number with a limit you choose, below the model’s [context window](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows).
- **Context compaction:** Automatic context compaction (triggered at ~135k tokens) to support long-running, multi-turn sessions without losing context or hitting token limits.
If the last `assistant` turn ends in a tool call with no result yet, the API rejects the request. Send that turn’s tool results first.

practices.statement: After compaction, send the lab's compaction item back unchanged and re-send what it does not carry: tools added mid-conversation on OpenAI, the system prompt placed right after the item on xAI, and mid-conversation instructions or effort level on Anthropic. Re-derive those from the controller's own records, not from the summary.
practices.why: OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic each say not to alter the compaction output and each name something the item leaves out.
practices.today: For the one model with compaction, the history is replaced by the single signed block the API returned. The survey does not say what is re-sent after the block, and there is no compaction for OpenAI or xAI seats.

basis.quote: Output handling: do not prune `/responses/compact` output. The returned window is the canonical next context window, so pass it into your next `/responses` call as-is.

A compaction item has to come first, because the API drops anything before it, `instructions` included. So the system prompt stays out of the compaction and goes right after the item, which keeps the handbook word for word however often the chat is compacted.
The block holds the summary as text you can read, and a signature. Send it in future requests exactly as it came.

The explicit trigger's compaction item doesn't carry earlier `additional_tools` declarations. If you resume from that item, supply the tools you need in the request's `tools` array or append a new developer `additional_tools` item before the user message.
If an instruction or effort level still matters, state it again in a `role: "system"` message.

practices.statement: Carry work between stages and sessions through the signed ledgers, not through conversation or compacted state. Derive each stage's handoff from the ledger, include decisions, abandoned approaches with their reasons and unresolved items, and re-check a carried fact's version before a passed stage or review is reused.
practices.why: OpenAI says to keep facts that matter in reviewed artifacts instead of compacted state or memory, and Anthropic says a clean handoff depends on the artifact holding enough state, including failed approaches, and that a stale note is trusted by a later session.
practices.today: Each stage re-derives its handoff from the work ledger and a passed stage is reused only while its chain to a valid plan holds, with a test; the plan handoff carries justification, exclusions, findings, unproven items and unresolved findings. Review citations are not re-checked before a review is reused, and the module that records abandoned paths with reasons has no importer outside its tests.

basis.quote: Keep cited facts in generated artifacts, not only in compacted conversation state.

While compaction preserves continuity, it doesn't give the agent a clean slate, which means context anxiety can still persist. A reset provides a clean slate, at the cost of the handoff artifact having enough state for the next agent to pick up the work cleanly.
The failed approaches are important—without them, successive sessions will re-attempt the same dead ends.

Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
Treat memories as a helpful recall layer, not as the only source for rules that must always apply.

practices.statement: Pass a researcher's or subagent's work to later seats as a bounded summary with the material conclusions first, and keep the full report in durable storage outside the prompt.
practices.why: OpenAI and Anthropic both say subagents should return summaries so the main context does not grow by the raw output, and Anthropic says to store the full record durably so discarded context stays recoverable.
practices.today: Research findings reach later seats as one derived dossier view bounded at 6,000 bytes with material conclusions first, while the full member reports stay on the work ledger and in the item's state. The survey shows this in code.

basis.quote: Return **summaries** from subagents instead of raw intermediate output.
A subagent returns only its final response, so your main agent's context grows by a summary, not by the subtask's transcript.

Ask the main agent to keep the goal and schedule, delegate each task to a subagent, and retain a short result. This keeps detailed tool output from repeated checks out of the main session's context window.

We separated the concerns of recoverable context storage in the session and arbitrary context management in the harness because we can’t predict what specific context engineering will be required in future models.

themes.title: How hard a model thinks
themes.covers: The reasoning or thinking control: when to raise or lower it, defaults, and what it costs.

agree.point: All four labs describe effort as a trade: a higher level buys deeper reasoning and possibly better results on complex work, and costs latency and tokens.

basis.quote: Lower effort favors speed and lower token usage, while at higher effort the model thinks more completely to provide higher quality responses.
| `"xhigh"` | Maximum reasoning depth, with correspondingly higher latency | The hardest problems, where answer quality matters more than response time |
Thinking models generate internal reasoning tokens to improve quality. This reasoning process increases both response latency and total token consumption.
`effort` trades latency and token cost for reasoning depth within each response.
Higher reasoning effort increases response time and token usage, but it can improve quality for complex work.

Before switching to a larger or smaller model, tune [`thinking_level`](/docs/thinking#thinking-levels). Thinking level sets how much internal reasoning a model performs before answering, which controls latency and token spend.
Lower effort is faster and cheaper for straightforward tasks, while higher effort provides deeper reasoning for complex problems.

agree.point: All four labs say to set the effort level explicitly instead of taking a default, because the default differs between models and changes when a model is swapped.

basis.quote: Set the effort explicitly on every request so a default never decides your result, and choose the effort you intend to run in production. If cost or latency matters, compare effort levels and weigh quality against tokens and time.
- inheriting 5.6's default `medium` reasoning where the old effective effort was `none`;

* **Configure `thinking_level`:** Hydrogen defaults to `high` rather than `medium`, adds `xhigh`, and rejects `minimal` with an error. Test `medium` and `high` on your evaluation suite to balance speed and cost.
Set `effort` explicitly: the default is `medium`, where Claude Opus 5’s is `high`.
The supported values and the default depend on the model; `grok-4.7` defaults to `"high"`, while `grok-4.3` defaults to `"low"` and also accepts `"none"`.
- A previously omitted setting can therefore become slower, more expensive, and incompatible with Chat Completions function tools after the model swap.
Most Claude models default to high effort, spending as many tokens as needed for excellent results; Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 default to medium.

agree.point: All four labs say to choose the level by running your own evaluations at more than one level and keeping the lowest one that holds quality, not by intuition.

basis.quote: 4. After the baseline passes, test the same setting and one lower on representative tasks.

More reasoning doesn't always pay off. On the sample's short tickets, medium, high, and xhigh used about the same number of reasoning tokens, around 600 per answer, so they cost about the same. Low used about 140 and cost half as much.
Run your evaluations at all four levels with a high `max_output_tokens` so the limit doesn't cut answers short, then pick the lowest `thinking_level` that meets your quality bar.
There’s no fixed mapping from a budget to an effort level, so run your evaluations at two or three levels.
- Reasoning effort selection, where higher effort is not always better and the right choice depends on task shape, not intuition
That step also uses more tokens and more time, so move down to `medium` wherever your evals hold. Above `high`, gains are uneven and task-dependent.

agree.point: All four labs reserve the top levels (xhigh, max) for the hardest problems, and OpenAI, Google and Anthropic add that they should not be a default and can overthink simple tasks.

basis.quote: - Reserve max for the hardest quality-first workloads; do not recommend it globally.
| `"xhigh"` | Maximum reasoning depth, with correspondingly higher latency | The hardest problems, where answer quality matters more than response time |
Start with `high` for most complex tasks, and reserve `xhigh` for hard, multi-step problems where `high` falls short.
On most workloads `max` adds significant cost for relatively small quality gains, and on some structured-output or less intelligence-sensitive tasks it can lead to overthinking.
- `xhigh`: Avoid as a default unless your evals show clear benefits. It is best suited for long, agentic, reasoning-heavy tasks where maximum intelligence matters more than speed or cost.
Using `xhigh` increases latency and token use and can cause overthinking or exhaust `max_output_tokens` on simpler prompts such as text or JSON extraction.
`max` may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking, so test before adopting it broadly

agree.point: All four labs bill reasoning tokens, and OpenAI, Google and Anthropic state that this holds even when the reasoning text is not returned.

basis.quote: While reasoning tokens are not visible via the API, they still occupy space in the model's context window and are billed as [output tokens](https://openai.com/api/pricing).
When you use a reasoning model, the reasoning tokens are billed as part of your total consumption.
Pricing is based on the full thought tokens the model needs to generate, despite only the summary being output from the API.
Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens even when the thinking text is not returned to you, so such a workload can produce more output tokens per request.
You are charged for all thinking tokens generated, even when collapsed or redacted.

agree.point: OpenAI, Google and Anthropic say to reduce thinking by lowering the effort level, not by a small output-token cap, because a cap reached during reasoning returns truncated or empty output that is still billed.

basis.quote: This might occur before any visible output tokens are produced, meaning you could incur costs for input and reasoning tokens without receiving a visible response.
To reduce cost or latency without truncating responses, lower `thinking_level` (`low` or `medium`) instead of setting a small `max_output_tokens`.

To spend fewer tokens on thinking, lower the [effort](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort) level. If you run at `xhigh` or `max` effort, set a large `max_tokens` so the model has room to think and act; start at 64k tokens and tune from there.

Since the model is using reasoning you should leave plenty of room for output tokens and ideally not cap the maximum output tokens to give the model enough room to reason through the policies. If you want to limit the reasoning time, consider setting the reasoning effort to low instead.
If the model hits this limit while reasoning, it stops generating with status `"incomplete"` and returns truncated or empty output (while still billing for any thinking tokens generated).
Lowering it doesn't make the model think more concisely, and instead cuts the response off sooner.
Thinking tokens count toward `max_tokens`, so a request with a small `max_tokens` can stop with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` after a `thinking` block and before any text.

agree.point: All four labs point low effort at simple, well-scoped or latency-sensitive steps such as picking the next tool, classification or a single search.

basis.quote: Efficient reasoning with a modest latency increase. Ideal for use cases requiring tool-use, planning, search, or multi-step decision making, while optimizing for speed and cost.
| `"low"` | Uses some reasoning tokens, but still fast | Latency-sensitive agentic use and simple tool calling. |
- **Simple tasks**: Use minimal thinking for fact retrieval or classification (e.g., "Where was DeepMind founded?").
`low` suits quick back-and-forth, well-specified tasks, and high-volume workloads (intelligent and fast subagents, for example).
**`low`**: Use when the task is straightforward and speed matters most.

Each turn uses a low reasoning effort, since it only picks the next tool or writes a short email. When we tried the refund decision at the default effort, it took 15 to 47 seconds instead of 2 to 9, and came to the same $48.00.
Lower thinking levels generally achieve a good balance for standard automation tasks.
Use lower effort for agents doing simple, well-scoped tasks, such as listing files or running a single grep, to reduce cost and latency.

agree.point: All four labs report that too little effort on multi-step agent work makes the model skip steps or checks or stop early, and that more effort keeps it on the task through its checks.

basis.quote: Higher reasoning effort can help the model stick with a long-running task through the final checks, even when the answer you need is only a few lines.

Grok uses medium reasoning effort. At low effort, it skipped the skill's steps and wrote the fix and the test in the same turn, so the test never failed first. At medium, a turn takes a few seconds and Grok follows the steps.
* For autonomous subagents with tool calls, code execution, or multi-step reasoning: set `thinking_level` to `"medium"` or `"high"` to prevent premature tool termination.
In long agent prompts, the model is more likely to skip a search, stop early, or skip a check at `low`.
In tests on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1, Claude at a higher level tested more edge cases and verified more of its work before answering. It also made more choices on its own.

agree.point: OpenAI, Google and Anthropic say that a harness managing its own history must send back the model's reasoning items or thought blocks unchanged during tool use.

basis.quote: Preserve and replay every returned reasoning item. Each item includes `encrypted_content` by default when you create a response.
* You **MUST** always resend all `thought` blocks exactly as they were received from the model.
With tool use, pass back every `thinking` and `redacted_thinking` block from the assistant turn exactly as received, including blocks whose `thinking` field is empty.
Persisting these reasoning items between tool calls during inference will therefore lead to higher intelligence and performance in the form of better decision in when and how a tool gets called.
If your application filters content blocks by type before resending, include both `thinking` and `redacted_thinking`.

differ.point: The default level is not the same anywhere: OpenAI treats medium as the default and starting point; xAI's current models default to high while grok-4.3 defaults to low; Google thinks dynamically by default and Gemini 4 Hydrogen defaults to high; Anthropic's API defaults most models to high and Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 to medium. Anthropic's own product differs from its API: Claude Code runs Fable 5.2 at medium where the API default is high.

basis.quote: Default configuration for most workloads, and a well-balanced point on the pareto curve of latency, performance and cost.
If not specified, `reasoning_effort` defaults to `"high"`. Reasoning cannot be disabled.

Gemini models engage in dynamic thinking by default, automatically adjusting the amount of reasoning effort based on the complexity of the request. You can control this behavior using the `thinking_level` parameter.
Most Claude models default to high effort, spending as many tokens as needed for excellent results; Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 default to medium.
- **Reasoning effort:** Start with `medium` for a new integration. If you currently use `none` or `minimal`, use `low` instead.

agree.point: Give the model only the tools the task needs and keep the active set small, because every definition takes context and selection gets worse as candidates grow; when the library is large, defer definitions behind tool search or retrieval.

basis.quote: Expose only task-relevant tools. Tool descriptions should state what the tool does, when to use it, important return fields, and error behavior.

Every function declaration you send is billed as input tokens on every request, and tool selection accuracy declines as the number of candidates grows. Once you pass roughly 20 to 30 tools, consider [tool retrieval](/docs/tool-retrieval).

**Filter tools appropriately**: Use `allowed_tools` to restrict access to only necessary tools, especially when servers have many tools since the model must keep all available tool definitions in context

One of the most common failure modes we see is bloated tool sets that cover too much functionality or lead to ambiguous decision points about which tool to use. If a human engineer can’t definitively say which tool should be used in a given situation, an AI agent can’t be expected to do better.
- **Use tool search** to defer large or infrequently used parts of your tool surface instead of exposing everything up front.

For best results, aim to provide only the relevant tools for the context or task, ideally keeping the active set to a maximum of 10-20. Consider dynamic tool selection based on conversation context if you have a large total number of tools.
This trades a small amount of latency (one extra turn to look up a tool) for a large reduction in baseline context usage.

agree.point: The model picks and fills a tool from its description, so each description must say clearly what the tool does and when to call it.

basis.quote: Expose only task-relevant tools. Tool descriptions should state what the tool does, when to use it, important return fields, and error behavior.
| `description` | No | What the tool does. Treated as empty if omitted; a clear description helps the model decide when to use it |
* **Function and Parameter Descriptions:** Be extremely clear and specific in your descriptions. The model relies on these to choose the correct function and provide appropriate arguments.
**Provide extremely detailed descriptions.** This is by far the most important factor in tool performance.
- **Explicitly describe the purpose of the function and each parameter** (and its format), and what the output represents.

basis.quote: - **Use enums** and object structure to prevent invalid states. For example, `toggle_light(on: bool, off: bool)` allows for invalid calls.
* **Strong Typing:** Use specific types (integer, string, enum) for parameters to reduce errors. If a parameter has a limited set of valid values, use an enum.
For classification tasks, use either tools with an enum field containing your valid labels or structured outputs.
When in doubt we recommend you err on the side of making the arguments flat.
* **Flatten nested objects and bound recursion:** Replace deeply nested object hierarchies with flatter structures.
**Simplify nested structures.** Deeply nested objects with optional fields compound the complexity. Flatten structures where possible.

agree.point: Return a failed tool call to the model as an error result with a message it can act on, so it can correct the call or retry.

basis.quote: If a command fails or times out, return its outcome so the model can decide whether to retry.
Return informative error messages that the model can use to generate helpful responses to the user.

A refused or failed query comes back as a tool result with `isError: true`, so Grok reads why and can fix its SQL. The tools also carry the `readOnlyHint` annotation, but that's a hint for clients, and nothing relies on it.

Write instructive error messages. Instead of generic errors such as `"failed"`, include what went wrong and what Claude should try next (for example, `"Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds."`).
For an error, set `success: false` and supply an `error` message that the agent can use.

Similarly, if a tool call raises an error (for example, during input validation), you can prompt-engineer your error responses to clearly communicate specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks.

agree.point: A schema fixes the shape of an output, not its correctness: the application must still validate values and handle refusals, incomplete responses and schema keywords the lab does not enforce.

basis.quote: Your application still needs to handle refusals, incomplete responses, and API errors, and validate any business rules that the schema does not express.
* **Validation:** While output is syntactically correct JSON, always validate values in your application.

These keywords are accepted but not structurally enforced; the model handles them and does so reliably in practice, but outputs are not guaranteed to satisfy these constraints. We recommend validating if strict conformance is required.

Unlike `zodOutputFormat()`, it doesn’t validate the response, so it doesn’t catch violations of [constraints not supported by the API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs#json-schema-limitations), such as `minimum`.

If these keywords are present in your schema (for instance, emitted automatically by Pydantic's `Field(min_length=...)` or Zod's `.min()`), the API automatically strips and ignores them during request normalization rather than returning an error.
The output might not match your schema because the refusal message takes precedence over schema constraints.

agree.point: Function calling is for intermediate actions against your own systems, and structured output is for the shape of the model's final response.

basis.quote: Conversely, Structured Outputs via `response_format` are more suitable when you want to indicate a structured schema for use when the model responds to the user, rather than when the model calls a tool.

Use [Function calling](/docs/function-calling) when the model needs to perform an intermediate step by connecting to your own tools or data systems. Use [Structured Outputs](/docs/structured-output) when you strictly need the model's final response to adhere to a specific schema, such as for rendering a custom UI.
**JSON outputs** control Claude’s response format (what Claude says).

agree.point: One response can carry several tool calls among other items, so the handler must read items by type rather than position, run every call, and return a result for each call matched by its id.

basis.quote: Since model responses can include zero, one, or multiple calls, it is best practice to assume there are several.
By default, parallel function calling is enabled — the model can request multiple tool calls in a single response. Process all of them before continuing:

Because of this, don't assume the `functionCall` will always be the last item in the parts array. If you are manually parsing the JSON response, always iterate through the parts array rather than relying on position.
Add a `user` message with one `tool_result` block for each `tool_use` block in that content, even if the tool failed.
In Responses, tool calls and their outputs are two distinct types of Items that are correlated using a `call_id`.

The Gemini API maps each result back to its corresponding call using the `id` from the model's output. This lets you execute your functions asynchronously and append the results to your list as they complete.
Select content blocks by their `type` field instead: read `text` from the blocks whose `type` is `"text"`, and branch on the block type when handling stream events.

agree.point: Tool results should be compact and structured, carrying only the fields the next step needs, with large payloads cut, paginated or passed by reference.

basis.quote: - Return structured, compact data that JavaScript can inspect without parsing prose.

Return semantic, stable identifiers (for example, slugs or UUIDs) rather than opaque internal references, and include only the fields Claude needs to reason about its next step. Bloated responses waste context and make it harder for Claude to extract what matters.

Inline data counts toward the request size limit. For large files, such as videos, long audio, or multi-page documents, upload the file with the [Files API](/docs/files) and return its `uri` instead of inline `data`.
The baseline returns oversized payloads to show how tool outputs can dominate input tokens; later rounds return only fields needed for the decision and response.
We suggest implementing some combination of pagination, range selection, filtering, and/or truncation with sensible default parameter values for any tool responses that could use up lots of context.

basis.quote: A refused or failed query comes back as a tool result with `isError: true`, so Grok reads why and can fix its SQL. The tools also carry the `readOnlyHint` annotation, but that's a hint for clients, and nothing relies on it.
Annotations are metadata, not enforcement. A tool marked `readOnlyHint: true` can still write to disk if that's what the handler does. Keep the annotation accurate to the handler.
All fields are optional hints; clients should not rely on them for security decisions.

agree.point: OpenAI and Anthropic both say to start with one agent or the simplest design and to add agents or a second model only when a specific need or a measurement justifies it.

basis.quote: Define the smallest agent that can own a clear task. Add more agents only when you need separate ownership, different instructions, different tool surfaces, or different approval policies.
When building applications with LLMs, we recommend finding the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed. This might mean not building agentic systems at all.
The decision to use a multi-agent architecture should be driven by your evals. Starting with a multi-agent architecture adds unnecessary complexity that can slow down your time to production.
Tune one model before you add a second: sweep effort on your current model first, because most workloads end there, and if the sweep shows a gap, price the stronger model alone at low effort.

agree.point: OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI all say more agents use more tokens, and OpenAI and Anthropic say delegation does not pay for work that is one dependent chain.

basis.quote: Note that adding subagents can increase token usage, and may not be as beneficial for tasks that depend on a single ordered chain of reasoning, require frequent writes to shared mutable state, or are already dominated by one slow external operation.

In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance.

You can configure how many agents collaborate on a request. The two available setups are **4 agents** and **16 agents**. More agents means deeper, more thorough research at the cost of higher token usage and latency.
Because each subagent does its own model and tool work, subagent workflows consume more tokens than comparable single-agent runs.

Worktrees let Codex run multiple independent chats in the same project without interfering with each other.
When you have separate pieces of work going at once, give each its own checkout so the edits can't collide.

agree.point: OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic describe a subagent as a separate context that does not receive the parent's whole conversation and that hands a summary or final result back.

basis.quote: Each subagent has its own context and can work in parallel with the others. The main agent coordinates their work and combines their results.
Subagents are independent child sessions with their own context. They return a summary to the parent when finished. Enabled by default when the setting is unset.
Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read.

practices.today: A turn is accepted only on status completed (Responses), stop reason end_turn, tool_use or stop_sequence (Messages), or finish reason STOP and not blocked (Gemini); a state the provider did not report is not a success. practices.statement: Set the output cap per lab and per model from a recorded fact, and derive it again at every model change. For OpenAI keep it near the expected response size, because the cap counts toward the rate limit; for Anthropic size it generously and add headroom after a tokenizer change; for Gemini 4 remove low caps and lower the thinking level to save tokens; for xAI set it above the longest expected answer.

practices.today: Caps come from difficulty tiers (4,096, 16,384 and 32,768 tokens, or five tiers from 1,024 to 65,536 under fit), each capped at the model's documented ceiling. The tiers file calls them provisional and not a measurement, and the survey shows no per-lab rule.

practices.statement: Build every seat's request with stable content first (tool definitions, role instructions, shared reference material) and per-unit text, timestamps and ledger state last. Then set each lab's own control: a per-conversation prompt_cache_key for xAI, a cache_control breakpoint at the end of the static prefix for Anthropic, and no explicit cache objects for Gemini 4, which caches only implicitly.
practices.why: All four labs say a stable prefix placed first is what makes a request cacheable, but the control differs: xAI routes by cache key, Anthropic marks the end of the reusable content, and Gemini 4 does not support explicit caching.
practices.today: Caching is limited to identifiers and pass-through: a Responses request gets a prompt_cache_key hashed from scope, session, vendor and model, cache_control is an allowed pass-through field on Messages that a search finds nothing else using, and Gemini cachedContent is deleted from the config. **Latency-sensitive paths first** — Priority Processing is most valuable for user-facing requests where response time directly affects experience. Background jobs, evaluations, and bulk processing are better served by the [Batch API](/developers/advanced-api-usage/batch-api).
